title: Częstochowa
hook: Poland's Black Madonna, an icon with scars on her cheek

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Akathist: a long hymn to Mary that the Byzantine churches sing on their feet. Your line was sung standing. Did you stand for anything, or anyone, yesterday? Day one thousand three hundred forty-two.

Two thin cuts run down a woman's right cheek. They aren't on a statue or a person. They're on a painting: a dark icon of Mary holding her child, kept in a monastery on a hill in the Polish city of Częstochowa. Her face is solemn and dark brown, almost black, which is why people call her the Black Madonna. Her son sits on her arm, one hand raised. And across her cheek, plain to anyone who stands in front of her, are those two lines and a third crossing them, like a scar that healed badly. A precious image, guarded and honored, and nobody has made it look new. Why would anyone keep the wound? Today's word is the city.
screen: `TWO CUTS ON A PAINTED CHEEK.` → `THE BLACK MADONNA.` → `WHY KEEP THE WOUND?`

segments.voice: Start with the stories, because this icon comes wrapped in them. Tradition says Saint Luke painted it, on a tabletop from the house in Nazareth. Art historians argue about when and where the painting was really made. Catholics are free to hold the legend lightly; it's a story people tell, not something the Church asks anyone to believe. Then the scars. Tradition says raiders once broke into the monastery, tried to carry the icon off, and when it wouldn't go, one of them struck her face with a sword. The image was repaired, but the cuts were left, or came back, depending on who tells it. And the dark color? Smoke from candles, age, the paint itself. People still debate it. Next, the country. Tradition says that when the monastery held out against an invading army, Poland's king named Mary queen of Poland. Through wars and hard years after that, Poles kept coming to this hill. Pilgrims still walk there on foot, singing as they go. Which brings us back to the scars. In the Book of Lamentations, a ruined city speaks to everyone who walks past her. In the Douay-Rheims: "O all ye that pass by the way, attend, and see if there be any sorrow like to my sorrow." Some readers have heard Mary in that voice. A pilgrim standing before this icon does what the verse asks: stops, and looks at the wound. So a mother with a sword cut on her face isn't damage to be hidden. For pilgrims from a country that knew invasion, she could be a mother who had been hurt too, and stayed.
screen: `A LEGEND, HELD LIGHTLY.` · `THE CUTS WERE LEFT.` · `A COUNTRY KEEPS COMING BACK.` · `ATTEND, AND SEE.` · then, large: `SEE IF THERE BE ANY SORROW LIKE TO MY SORROW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for Poland. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the country, or one person from it: a neighbor, a coworker, a grandmother, a name you know. Think of the pilgrims on the road to that hill, tired, singing, walking toward a scarred face. Then let your mind move to anyone you know who carries a wound that hasn't been painted over. If you pray, you can say a Hail Mary for Poland and for them. If you don't, simply hold them in mind, kindly, for the length of the sit. The bell holds the time.
Częstochowa. The Polish city whose monastery keeps the Black Madonna, an icon of Mary with scars across her cheek, honored as a mother by the pilgrims who walk to it. Today's word.
Your line: the scarred icon. Today, notice one thing, or one person, whose worth shows in the marks it carries, and don't wish the marks away. Day one thousand three hundred forty-two.

howItsDone: Catholics venerate the icon of Our Lady of Częstochowa at the Jasna Góra monastery in Poland, where pilgrims come to pray before it, some walking there on foot, and copies of the icon hang in Polish churches and homes elsewhere.

what a scholar hears: two histories at once: the legend of Saint Luke, and art historians' unsettled debate about when and where the painting was made.

sources.ref: Traditions of the icon of Our Lady of Częstochowa (Jasna Góra): Saint Luke as painter, the sword cuts, the siege and Mary named queen of Poland

notes: Editor: replaced Simeon's sword (Luke 2:35, already quoted on day 1333) with Lamentations 1:12 in the teach, screen, match, myth, fork and sources; cut 'some of them for days' (unsourced count); softened the Polish-history line to pilgrims rather than a whole people.

All historical details are given as 'tradition says': Saint Luke painting it on a Nazareth tabletop; raiders striking the face with a sword (often dated to a Hussite raid in 1430); the siege of Jasna Góra and the king naming Mary queen of Poland (usually linked to John II Casimir's vows of 1656). No dates are stated. Confirm phrasing.
Description of the cuts: 'two thin cuts and a third crossing them' on the right cheek. Confirm the usual description of the scars.
'Repaired, but the cuts were left, or came back, depending on who tells it' reflects two versions of the story (restorers kept them; a legend that repainting failed). Confirm fair.
Reasons for the dark color (candle smoke, age, pigment) are given as debated. Confirm.
Claim that pilgrims walk on foot 'some of them for days' refers to the walking pilgrimages (e.g. from Warsaw); no numbers given. Confirm.
The practice offers a Hail Mary 'if you pray'; no new prayer written.

Douay-Rheims (Challoner) Lamentations 1:12 wording: confirm 'O all ye that pass by the way, attend, and see if there be any sorrow like to my sorrow.' 'Some readers have heard Mary in that voice' attributes the Marian reading; confirm.
